Style and usage A–Z
Numbers
2-byte character  Don’t use; use double-byte character.
2D  Abbreviation for two-dimensional. No hyphen in the abbreviation. For guidelines about 
spelling out abbreviations, see abbreviations and acronyms.
2K, 4K, 5K, 6K, 8K (adj.)  Horizontal screen resolution or image resolution measured in 
thousands of pixels. Don’t use a space between the numeral and the K.
The 27-inch iMac has a Retina 5K display.
Apple ProRes codecs support all standard frame sizes (including SD, 
HD, 2K, and 4K).
3D  Abbreviation for three-dimensional. No hyphen in the abbreviation. For guidelines 
about spelling out abbreviations, see abbreviations and acronyms.
3D Touch  A technology used in some older iPhone models that lets users access 
additional features by pressing the display. Newer models use Haptic Touch. See also 
Force Touch; Haptic Touch; press. 
10Base-T, 100Base-T, 1000Base-T  Note capitalization. See also Ethernet; Fast Ethernet 
(100Base-T); Gigabit Ethernet (1000Base-T).
24/7  Not 24x7. To spell out, use the form 24 hours a day, 7 days a week; a 24-hour-a-day, 
7-day-a-week support program.
A
AAC  Abbreviation for Advanced Audio Coding, an industry-standard audio compression 
format. For guidelines about spelling out abbreviations, see abbreviations and acronyms.
abbreviations and acronyms  An acronym is a pronounceable word formed from the initial 
letter or letters of major parts of a compound term. An abbreviation is usually formed 
in the same way but isn’t pronounced as a word. Abbreviations are often lowercase or a 
mix of lowercase and uppercase. Acronyms are almost always all caps, regardless of the 
capitalization style of the spelled-out form.
Abbreviation: mph—for miles per hour; MB/s—for megabytes per second
Acronym: ROM—for read-only memory
11
Apple Style Guide
•	 When to spell out: If you think your audience might not be familiar with an abbreviation 
or acronym, spell out its first occurrence on a page or in a section. In user materials, 
spell out the term when you introduce it.
•	 How to spell out: When you spell out a term, generally put the spelled-out version first, 
with the abbreviation or acronym in parentheses.
internet service provider (ISP)
If the abbreviation or acronym is much more familiar than the spelled-out version, 
you can put the abbreviation or acronym first, followed by the spelled-out version in 
parentheses, or you can explain that the abbreviation is “short for” the spelled-out 
version and place the spelled-out version in italics.
You can share your personal URL (Uniform Resource Locator).
An internet address is sometimes called a URL, short for Uniform 
Resource Locator.
•	 File types: Use all caps for abbreviations of file types.
a JPEG file, an AIFF file, the MP3 file
Filename extensions, which indicate the file type, should be in lowercase.
.jpg, .aif, .mp3, .iba
See also filename extensions; file types.
•	 Pronunciation: If you think the reader might not know how to pronounce the acronym, 
provide a pronunciation key.
WYSIWYG (pronounced “WIZ-zee-wig”)
See also pronunciation.
•	 Articles: Use the article a or an with an abbreviation or acronym, depending on its 
pronunciation.
a SAN, a USB port, an FAQ, an LCD screen
•	 Punctuation: Don’t use periods except in abbreviations for nonmetric units of measure 
and in the abbreviations a.m., p.m., and U.S. (see U.S. for exception).
•	 Plural: Don’t add an apostrophe before the s when you form the plural of an 
abbreviation.
CDs, ICs, ISPs
•	 Latin: Avoid using Latin abbreviations.
Correct: for example, and others, and so on, and that is, or equivalent 
phrases
Incorrect: e.g. (for example), et al. (and others), etc. (and so on), i.e. 
(that is)
•	 Units of measure: See Units of measure for detailed usage guidelines.
•	 Product names: Don’t abbreviate any Apple product or service names, whether or not 
the product or service is trademarked or has a service mark.
abort  Avoid in user materials. See also exit; interrupt; quit; stop.
12
Apple Style Guide
above, below  You can use above or below to describe text or an object that closely 
precedes or follows the current paragraph.
In the example above, clip B is shortened and clip C is lengthened, but 
their combined duration stays the same. [earlier figure]
These sliders mirror the settings of the Levels sliders, described 
above. [earlier text]
The diagram below shows a typical network configuration. [later figure]
The process for creating a multicam project is outlined below. [later 
text]
Otherwise, use a cross-reference (consult your department’s guidelines about the style of 
cross-references).
See also cross-references.
AC  Abbreviation for alternating current. For guidelines about spelling out abbreviations, 
see abbreviations and acronyms.
AC adapter  Don’t use; use power adapter. See also adapter; power adapter.
access (n., v.)  It’s OK to use access as a verb when you can’t be more specific. Even in 
developer materials, consider more precise terms, such as log in to.
Avoid: Access the server using an administrator account.
Preferable: Log in to the server using an administrator account.
Avoid: You can access the internet with your MacBook Air.
Preferable: You can connect to the internet with your MacBook Air.
accessibility  Refers to features that enable people with disabilities to successfully use 
Apple products and services. Capitalize the names of accessibility features. For example:
Accessibility Keyboard, AssistiveTouch, Guided Access, Hover Text, 
Invert Colors, Larger Dynamic Type, Live Listen, Magnifier, Safari 
Reader, Speak Screen, Speak Selection, Switch Control, Text to Speech, 
Type to Siri, Typing Feedback, Voice Control, VoiceOver, Zoom
See also Writing about disability.
access point  Also called a wireless access point. A device, such as a base station, that 
transmits and receives data in a wireless network. See also AirPort.
Access Point Name  See APN.
acronyms  See abbreviations and acronyms.
action  A component of an Automator workflow. A workflow is an entire task. Each action is 
a specific part of the task (such as opening a new message in Mail).
Action button  Note capitalization.
Choose a function for the Action button.
action description  In Automator, the description of the selected workflow action.
13
Apple Style Guide
Action pop-up menu  A pop-up menu labeled with an ellipsis and a down arrow in the 
Finder and in some Mac apps.
See also More button.
action sheet  In iOS and iPadOS, refers to an alert that appears in response to a control or 
action and presents a set of two or more choices related to the current context.
In user materials, don’t use the term action sheet, sheet, or popover; instead, describe 
what the user must select or do.
Correct: Tap New Tab.
Incorrect: Tap New Tab in the sheet that appears.
In developer materials, action sheet is OK.
See also popover; share sheet; sheet.
activate, deactivate  Avoid; instead, use turn on, turn off.
active  Use to refer to the app or window currently being used. Preferred to in front. See 
also front, frontmost; in front.
Active Noise Cancellation  An AirPods feature. Use noise cancellation in general 
references.
You can switch between Active Noise Cancellation and Transparency 
mode.
When the fit of your AirPods is right, you experience better noise 
cancellation.
It’s OK to capitalize Noise Cancellation to match interface text.
Click the AirPods icon in the menu bar, then click Noise Cancellation.
After the first reference, you can abbreviate Active Noise Cancellation as ANC in AirPods 
model names.
AirPods 4 with Active Noise Cancellation feature a wireless charging 
case.
AirPods 4 (ANC) feature a wireless charging case.
Activity rings  Capitalize the names of the rings that track your daily activity in the Activity 
app (for example, Stand ring, Exercise ring).
14
Apple Style Guide
adapter  Not adaptor. Capitalize names of adapters that are sold separately.
Adaptive Audio  An AirPods feature. Don’t refer to as Adaptive mode.
Correct: You can customize Adaptive Audio to allow more or less noise.
Incorrect: You can customize Adaptive mode to allow more or less 
noise.
address  Can refer either to an internet address or to the location in the computer’s 
memory where a piece of information is stored. OK to use just address for either, as long 
as the context is clear. See also email addresses; internet addresses; memory address, 
memory location.
addresses (mailing)  Use the forms shown here for addresses. To include the country 
name in a U.S.-based Apple address, use USA (no periods).
•	 Apple corporate address: Use this form:
Apple [not Apple Inc.] 
One Apple Park Way
Cupertino, CA 95014
•	 Specific Apple mailing addresses:
Department Name
Apple
One Apple Park Way, MS xx-xx
Cupertino, CA 95014
•	 Other addresses: For other addresses, spell out elements such as Avenue, Drive, Road, 
Street, and Suite. It’s OK to abbreviate Blvd. and Bldg. Use the format shown in the 
preceding examples for city and state. Use two-letter abbreviations for state names 
(see The Chicago Manual of Style).
adjuster  Don’t use to refer to a control that has up and down arrows, or left and right 
arrows, to increase or decrease a value. In user materials, use up arrow, down arrow, 
right arrow, left arrow, or arrows, as appropriate. For example, Click one of the arrows to 
increase or decrease the volume. If it’s necessary to refer to the control itself, use stepper. 
See also stepper.
administrator (n.)  A person who has administrative authority for networks, servers, 
databases, or other information technology assets. Don’t shorten to admin.
To maintain the distinction between professional administrators and macOS users 
with administrator accounts, avoid using the noun administrator by itself to describe a 
person who has an administrator account in macOS. Instead, you can say a user with an 
administrator account—typically, the owner (or owners) of a particular Mac computer.
Correct: To obtain a static IP address for your computer, contact your 
network administrator.
Correct: You must have an administrator account to modify other user 
accounts on a Mac.
Incorrect: You must be an administrator to install software.
See also administrator (adj.); System Administrator.
15
Apple Style Guide
administrator (adj.)  Use in macOS to describe the primary account (or accounts) that 
can create other accounts, set access privileges, install software, and make systemwide 
settings. OK to shorten to admin in server and training materials. Don’t use the possessive 
form: administrator’s account, administrator’s password, or admin’s permissions.
Correct: Log in with an administrator account to install software.
Correct: To give a user broad privileges on a Mac, create an admin 
account for the user.
Incorrect: Log in with an administrator’s account to install software.
An administrator computer is a computer with macOS or macOS Server that you use to 
manage remote servers.
See also administrator (n.); standard user; System Administrator.
Advanced Video Coding High Definition  See AVCHD.
advisor, Advisor  Use Advisor to refer to a person in a customer-facing AppleCare Support 
position, including those at one of Apple’s outsourced vendor sites. Don’t use agent or 
representative. Use advisor if you’re not referring specifically to an AppleCare Support 
person.
College students can apply to be Apple At-Home Advisors.
AFP  Abbreviation for Apple Filing Protocol. For guidelines about spelling out abbreviations, 
see abbreviations and acronyms.
afterward  Not afterwards.
agent  Don’t use when referring to an AppleCare Support person. See also advisor, Advisor.
AirDrop  Don’t use as a verb.
Correct: You can use AirDrop to send photos, documents, and more to 
other Apple devices nearby.
Incorrect: You can AirDrop photos, documents, and more to other Apple 
devices nearby.
AirMac  The name for AirPort in Japan: AirMac wireless networking, AirMac Extreme Base 
Station, AirMac Express Base Station, and so on.
Airplane Mode  Note capitalization.
AirPlay  Don’t use as a verb.
Correct: You can use AirPlay to stream videos from iPhone to Apple TV.
Incorrect: You can AirPlay videos from iPhone to Apple TV.
AirPods  In general references, don’t use the with AirPods. It’s OK to use another article or 
a possessive adjective. If you need to refer to a specific pair of AirPods, it’s OK to use the.
Connect AirPods to a different device.
Use Find My to locate your AirPods.
Clean the AirPods you just tested, and then return them to the 
customer.
16
Apple Style Guide
Use numbers, not generation, to refer to models of AirPods—for example, AirPods Pro 2, 
not AirPods Pro (2nd generation).
When you write about a specific model of AirPods, use the model name: Learn how to 
clean your AirPods Max. You can use just AirPods if the content applies to any model: Use 
AirPods to make and answer calls with your iPhone.
Avoid using singular AirPod; instead, try to rewrite the sentence. If you do use singular 
AirPod, use the plural form of the name nearby, and don’t use it in a prominent location, 
such as a heading.
Avoid: You can change how each AirPod responds when you press or 
tap it.
Preferable: You can change how each of your AirPods responds when 
you press or tap it.
AirPort  Versions include AirPort, AirPort Extreme, and AirPort Time Capsule. You can use 
AirPort to refer generally to Apple’s wireless networking products or technologies or to 
refer to the family of AirPort products: your AirPort network, AirPort software.
•	 Software: AirPort software includes AirPort Utility and AirPort Disk Utility. Don’t precede 
these app names with the.
•	 Hardware: AirPort hardware includes the AirPort Express Base Station, the 
AirPort Extreme Base Station, and AirPort Time Capsule. You can shorten 
AirPort Express Base Station to AirPort Express, but don’t use AirPort Extreme unless 
you’re referring to the technology. Use an article or your with AirPort Express. Use 
lowercase for base station if you don’t use the full product name.
Correct: The AirPort Extreme Base Station is an Apple product.
Correct: Avoid placing the base station near sources of interference.
Incorrect: Avoid placing the Base Station near sources of interference.
alert (n., adj.)  Refers generically to a signal, either visual (a dialog) or auditory (a beep), 
that calls the user’s attention to an unusual situation. Visual alerts, such as the one shown 
here, provide messages about error conditions or warn users about potentially hazardous 
situations or actions.
17
Apple Style Guide
In user materials, you can use alert sound or alert message to describe generic alerts. 
Avoid error message except in developer materials.
The computer plays a sound (called the alert sound) when it needs your 
attention.
An alert message appears if a problem occurs during the installation.
In specific situations, however, avoid the word alert if you can simply describe what 
happens.
A message appears when the installation is finished.
alias  Use for with alias (not of or to).
The alias for the selected file is on the desktop.
The object the alias represents is called the original item. Don’t use aliased. See also email 
alias.
alignment  Use instead of justification to refer to the horizontal placement of lines of text 
with respect to the left and right edges of the margin. Alignment can be flush left, flush 
right, centered, or justified (that is, flush on both the left and right margins). See also 
justification.
all-in-one (adj.)  Refers to computers with built-in displays, such as iMac computers. Also 
refers to products that combine functions such as printing, faxing, scanning, and copying.
allow  Avoid using allow when you can restructure a sentence to make the reader the 
subject.
Avoid: FileMaker Pro allows you to create a database.
Preferable: You can create a database with FileMaker Pro.
See also enable (v.), enabled (adj.); let.
allow list  See deny list/allow list.
alphabet column  Don’t use to refer to the vertical column of letters at the right side of a 
list in some iOS apps; use index.
alphabetization  Alphabetize letter by letter, not word by word.
file format
filename
file server
widget
Wi-Fi
window
For detailed information about letter-by-letter alphabetizing, see The Chicago Manual of 
Style.
alphanumeric  One word.
18
Apple Style Guide
alternate (adj.), alternative (adj.)  Use alternate to mean every other or occurring or 
proceeding by turn. Use alternative to mean allowing two or more choices.
You can shade alternate rows of a table.
When traffic is heavy, Apple Maps provides alternative routes.
alternating current  See AC.
Alt key  Don’t use, except when you give instructions for Windows users. For Mac users,

of options, elements, rules, or instructions that need not be presented or performed in a

italics (n.), italic (adj.)  The noun form is plural.
Use italics to emphasize a word or phrase.
Use italic text to emphasize a word or phrase.
116
Apple Style Guide
Follow these guidelines for using italics:
•	 References to document titles: Italicize the entire title.
See the iPhone User Guide.

the i, the o’s
the word restart
the phrase Welcome to iOS 10

Make sure that the power cable is plugged in and that power is available

Choose File > Add Files to [app name].
•	 Terms that stand for or define other terms: Use italics, not quotation marks, for terms 
after stands for, labeled, named, termed, the term, and so on. If the term is an onscreen 
element, however, use plain text for elements whose names are capitalized title style; use 
plain text in quotation marks for elements whose names are capitalized sentence style.

font size  Not type size. When the meaning is clear, it’s OK to use just size.
font style  Not typestyle or typeface attribute. Refers to one or more attributes such as

foot  Note hyphenation when used as an adjective: 3-foot height, 3-foot-high table, but

use the symbol ′ unless space limitations prevent the use of foot or ft.
footnotes  See tables.

88

quotation marks  Use curly opening and closing quotation marks except in code font. Don’t 
use single or double quotation marks for units of measure; use the prime symbol for feet 
(Option-Shift-E) and the double prime symbol for inches (Option-Shift-G).
•	 With periods and commas: Put periods and commas within quotation marks. If 
necessary for clarity, periods and commas can go outside, as in AN$ = "1". 
•	 With other punctuation: Semicolons, colons, question marks, and exclamation points go 
outside quotation marks unless they’re part of an actual quotation.
•	 Four-character identifiers: When you give the name of four-character identifiers such as 
file types, use straight, single quotation marks in code font and place any punctuation 
outside the quotation marks.

•	 Terminology: Use quotation marks, not quote marks or quotes. (Quote is a verb;

•	 Cross-references and quotations: Cross-references to sections and chapter titles

Search for “Apps for college.”

ellipsis  A set of three dots indicating a continuation or, in a quotation, the omission of

username@domain

com domain.

background in your emails.

dash (em)  Use the em dash (—) to set off a word or phrase that interrupts or changes the 
direction of a sentence or to set off a lengthy list that would otherwise make the syntax of 
a sentence confusing. Don’t overuse em dashes. If the text being set off doesn’t come at

See all your schedules—work, school, and social life—in one app.

60
Apple Style Guide
dash (en)  The en dash (–) is shorter than an em dash and longer than a hyphen. Use the 
en dash as follows:
•	 Numbers in a range: Use an en dash between numbers that represent the endpoints of a

bits 3–17, 2003–2005

•	 Minus sign: Use an en dash as a minus sign (except in code font, where you use a

To generate an en dash, press Option-Hyphen. Close up the en dash with the word (or

Collective and thus singular: Data is stored in a FileMaker Pro database.

outside the quotation marks.

quotation marks.

background in your emails.

Press and hold the TV button 
.

C

I have enough now. Let me compile the findings that are actually relevant to this project.

Here's what's new and actionable from the full guide — things not already covered by DESIGN.MD:

---

**Typography & font terminology**
- Never say `typeface` — always `font`. Never say `type size` — always `font size` or just `size`. (Affects any UI copy or code comments.)
- Use `italics` as a noun (plural), `italic` as an adjective — "use italic text", not "use italics text".

**Capitalization on the site**
- The guide distinguishes two modes: **sentence-style** (only first word + proper nouns) and **title-style** (capitalize most words). For UI labels and nav items, Apple uses **sentence-style** — so nav items like "Worldbuilding", "Connections", "Books" are correct as-is since they're proper names/section titles, but any descriptive labels (eyebrows, footers, subtitles) should be sentence-style unless they're headings.
- The current footer text `"Eden, Third Heaven · Archive of the Throne of Wisdom"` is fine — it reads as a proper title.

**Buttons & links**
- Button labels should use **title-style** capitalization when not quoting an onscreen element (e.g. "Enter the Dominion", "Read the Writings" — not "Enter the dominion"). Currently `btn-primary` says "Enter the dominion" — **this should be title-style**: "Enter the Dominion".
- Don't use "follow a link" — use "click a link". Relevant if you write any body copy.

**Dashes**
- Em dash (—): no spaces around it, close it up with surrounding words. The footer `·` separator is fine.
- En dash (–): for ranges and compound adjectives with two-word elements. Currently all dashes on the site look correct.

**Quotation marks**
- Always **curly quotes** (`"` `"`) in UI text — never straight quotes. The hero quote already uses CSS `::before`/`::after` for curly quotes, so that's correct.
- Ellipsis: use the `…` character, not three periods.

## Additional Rules from Full Apple Style Guide (June 2025)

### **Font Terminology**

| Avoid | Use Instead |
|-------|-------------|
| `typeface` | `font` |
| `type size` | `font size` or just `size` |
| `type style` | `font style` or just `style` |
| `typestyle` | `font style` |
| `typeface attribute` | `font style` |

### **Italic vs Italics**

- `italic` — adjective: "use italic text", "italic font style"
- `italics` — noun (always plural): "use italics to emphasize", "the italics are applied"
- Never: "use italics text" or "an italics style"

**When to use italics in UI copy:**
- Document/work titles
- Letters as letters, words as words (`the word restart`, `the letter i`)
- Emphasis (use sparingly)
- Placeholder names (`[app name]`, `[volumeName]`)
- Terms being defined (`INIT stands for *initialize*`)
- Variables in technical notation

**When NOT to use italics:**
- Text the user actually types — use quotation marks or code font instead
- Onscreen element names in title-style capitalization — use plain text

### **Capitalization: Sentence-style vs Title-style**

**Sentence-style** (Apple default for UI labels, eyebrows, descriptive text):
- Capitalize only the first word and proper nouns/adjectives
- Use for: nav labels, filter chips, status tags, footer text, form labels, tooltips

**Title-style** (for button labels and section headings):
- Capitalize: first word, last word, nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, conjunctions (non-coordinating), prepositions ≥5 letters
- Don't capitalize: articles (`a`, `an`, `the`), coordinating conjunctions (`and`, `but`, `or`, `nor`, `for`, `yet`, `so`), `to` in infinitives, `as` (any part of speech), prepositions ≤4 letters (`at`, `by`, `for`, `from`, `in`, `of`, `on`, `to`, `up`, `with`)
- Exception: always capitalize prepositions that are part of a phrasal verb (`Turn On`, `Log In`, `Start Up`)

**Button labels always use title-style.** Examples:
- "Enter the Dominion" not "Enter the dominion"
- "Read the Writings" not "Read the writings"
- "Add to Favorites" not "Add to favorites"

### **Dashes**

| Dash | Character | Use | Spacing |
|------|-----------|-----|---------|
| Em dash | — | Interruption, parenthetical aside, list mid-sentence | No spaces — close up to adjacent words |
| En dash | – | Number ranges, compound adjectives with two-word element | No spaces — close up |
| Hyphen | - | Compound adjectives before noun, prefixes with exceptions | No spaces |

```
Correct:  See all your schedules—work, school, and social—in one app.
Correct:  bits 3–17,  2003–2005
Correct:  desktop interface–specific instructions
Incorrect: See all your schedules — work, school, and social — in one app.
```

### **Quotation Marks**

- Always curly/smart quotes (`"` `"`) in UI text — never straight (`"`)
- Periods and commas go **inside** closing quote marks
- Semicolons, colons, `?`, `!` go **outside** unless part of the actual quotation
- Use quotation marks to enclose sentence-style onscreen element names in documentation
- Use italics (not quotes) for terms being defined after *called*, *named*, *termed*, *stands for*
- Use the `…` ellipsis character — not three separate periods

### **Ellipsis**

- Use the single `…` character (not `...`) to prevent awkward line breaks between dots
- If a menu item or button name ends with `…`, omit it in running prose:
  - Correct: "Choose File > New and click a template."
  - Incorrect: "Choose File > New… and click a template."

### **Buttons & Links**

- Button labels: title-style capitalization
- "Click a link" — not "follow a link"
- "Click" for mouse/trackpad onscreen elements; "press" for physical/mechanical keys and buttons; "tap" for touchscreens
- Never: "hit", "push", "type" for keyboard keys (use "press")
- Never: "click on" — just "click"
- Don't use "click and drag" — you either click or drag

### **Web Terminology**

| Term | Rule |
|------|------|
| `homepage` | Entry point page only — not the whole site |
| `webpage` | One word; a single document within a site |
| `website` | The whole collection of pages |
| `web` | Lowercase (short for World Wide Web) |
| `web app`, `web browser`, `web server` | Two words |
| `webcam`, `webcast`, `webinar`, `webmail`, `webpage`, `website` | One word |
| `landing page`, `portal` | Don't use — use `homepage` |

### **Lists**

- Precede all lists with a colon (even if the intro is a partial sentence)
- All list items start with a capital letter (except product names that begin lowercase)
- List items that are complete sentences end with a period
- List items that are fragments: no terminal punctuation, or consistent punctuation throughout

## Core Style Parameters for Web Dev / CSS / JS

### **Typography & Text Formatting**

| Parameter | Rule |
|-----------|------|
| **Font style** | Use sentence-style capitalization for UI text, headings, labels |
| **Title-style caps** | Capitalize first/last word, nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs; lowercase articles, coordinating conjunctions, prepositions ≤4 letters |
| **Code font** | Fixed-width (Courier-like) for: user input, code listings, reserved words, literals, variables, commands in running text |
| **Body font for** | Punctuation following code font (unless part of the code element), file/folder names, system messages (paraphrased), URLs |
| **Italics** | Document titles, letters as letters, words as words, placeholder names, variables in code notation |
| **Quotation marks** | Curly quotes for UI elements in sentence-style; straight quotes in code font for 4-char identifiers |

### **Capitalization Rules (Critical for CSS class names, JS variables)**

```
/* Correct naming patterns */
.apple-menu        /* lowercase after first ref */
.command-key       /* lowercase generic */
.system-settings   /* lowercase generic refs */
/* Product names: exact official capitalization */
.iPad, .iPhone, .macOS, .iCloud, .AirPods, .AppleVisionPro
```

**Key rule**: *"Follow the style of the software itself for capitalization and spaces"* — this applies directly to CSS class naming and JS constants.

### **Hyphenation & Compound Words**

| Context | Pattern | Example |
|---------|---------|---------|
| Adjective before noun | Hyphenated | `user-friendly`, `built-in`, `third-party`, `full-screen`, `drag-and-drop` |
| Predicate adjective | No hyphen | `user friendly`, `built in`, `up to date` |
| Prefixes (auto, co, multi, non, pre, re, sub, super, ultra) | Close up | `autosave`, `coexist`, `multitasking`, `nonstandard`, `preinstalled`, `reenter`, `submenu`, `superfine`, `ultrafast` |
| Exceptions | Hyphenate before vowels, proper nouns, or if ambiguous | `co-op`, `anti-intellectual`, `re-create` |

### **Numbers & Units**

| Rule | Implementation |
|------|----------------|
| Spell out | 1–9 (cardinal), 0–9 (ordinal) |
| Use numerals | ≥10, addresses, bits/bytes/chapters, version numbers, units of measure, screen resolutions |
| No comma in | Memory addresses, microprocessor numbers |
| Range | En dash (–), full concluding number: `2013–2019`, `bits 3–17` |
| Software versions | No "version" or "v": `macOS 14`, `iOS 17.2`, not `macOS version 14` |

**CSS/JS implication**: Class names like `.8k-resolution`, `.5g-network` — no space between numeral and unit per guide.

### **Abbreviations & Acronyms**

| Rule | Web Dev Application |
|------|---------------------|
| Spell out first occurrence | `application programming interface (API)` |
| No periods | `HTML`, `CSS`, `JS`, `URL`, `API` (except `a.m.`, `p.m.`, `U.S.`) |
| Plural | Add `s` no apostrophe: `APIs`, `CSS modules`, `URLs` |
| File types | ALL CAPS: `JPEG`, `PNG`, `GIF`, `MP3`, `PDF` |
| Filename extensions | lowercase with dot: `.jpg`, `.png`, `.css`, `.js` |

### **Punctuation for Code/Technical Content**

| Element | Rule |
|---------|------|
| **Angle brackets** | `>` and `<` — use "left angle bracket"/"right angle bracket" or "less-than sign"/"greater-than sign" |
| **Braces** | `{}` — "braces", not "curly brackets" |
| **Brackets** | `[]` — "brackets", not "square brackets" |
| **Slash** | `/` — "slash" |
| **Colon in paths** | `Choose File > Export To > [format]` |
| **Keyboard shortcuts** | Hyphen for held-together: `Control-Shift-N`; no hyphen if pressed separately: `Esc N` |
| **Key order** | `Fn`, `Control`, `Option`, `Shift`, `Command` |

### **Critical "Don't Use" Terms for Web Dev**

| Avoid | Use Instead | Context |
|-------|-------------|---------|
| `blacklist`/`whitelist` | `deny list`/`allow list` | CSS class names, JS variables, API docs |
| `master`/`slave` | `primary`/`secondary`, `main`/`replica`, `host`/`client` | Git branches, database replication, component hierarchies |
| `dummy` | `placeholder`, `sample`, `test`, `stub` | Test data, mock objects |
| `sanity check` | `consistency check`, `logic check`, `final check` | Testing terminology |
| `grandfathered` | `legacy`, `exempt`, `preexisting` | Feature flags, compatibility modes |
| `disabled` (for features) | `turned off`, `unavailable` | Toggle states in UI |
| `enabled` (for features) | `turned on`, `selected`, `available` | Toggle states in UI |
| `hit` | `press`, `tap`, `click` | User actions |
| `abort` | `exit`, `interrupt`, `quit` | Error handling |
| `kill` | `force quit`, `terminate`, `end`, `stop` | Process management |
| `hang` | `not responding`, `stops responding` | Async operations |
| `crash` | `quits unexpectedly`, `stops responding` | Error reporting |

### **Accessibility & Inclusive Language (CSS/JS Implementation)**

| Parameter | Implementation |
|-----------|----------------|
| `autistic` (adj.) / `autism` (n.) | Use identity-first: "autistic person", not "person with autism" |
| `deaf`, `hard of hearing`, `deaf or hard of hearing` | Lowercase for general; capitalize `Deaf` for cultural identity |
| `blind`, `low vision` | "person who is blind", "person who has low vision" |
| `neurodivergent` / `neurodiverse` | Individual vs. group; never "neurodiverse" for one person |
| `wheelchair user` | Not "wheelchair-bound" or "confined to a wheelchair" |
| `they`/`them`/`their` | Singular gender-neutral pronoun acceptable |

### **Color & Visual Terminology**

| Rule | Application |
|------|-------------|
| `color blind` / `color blindness` | Not "colored" for screen elements; use specific color names |
| `grayscale` | One word |
| `black and white` (pred. adj.) / `black-and-white` (adj.) | Hyphenate before noun |
| Don't use `black`/`white` with positive/negative connotation | Only for actual color description |

### **Apple-Specific Product References (for Apple-targeted web dev)**

| Product | Rule |
|---------|------|
| `Apple Account` | Not `Apple ID` (as of June 2025) |
| `Apple Intelligence` | Don't abbreviate as `AI` in Apple contexts |
| `Apple silicon` | `Mac with Apple silicon`; not `Apple silicon Mac` |
| `M-series chips` | `M4`, `M4 Pro`, `M4 Max`; no `M4 chip` needed after first ref |
| `iPhone`, `iPad`, `Mac` | No article in general refs; OK with possessive or specific refs |
| `macOS` | Not `Mac OS`; features are `in macOS`, not `on macOS` |
| `iOS`, `iPadOS`, `tvOS`, `visionOS` | No article |
| `AirPods` | No `the`; use numbers not generation: `AirPods Pro 2` |

### **Code-Specific Notation**

| Element | Style |
|---------|-------|
| **Placeholder names** | Italic, lowercase, brackets: `[app name]`, `[volumeName]` |
| **Variables in text** | Italic: *volumeName* |
| **Syntax descriptions** | Code font for literals, plain text for variables |
| **Code listings** | Maintain language-standard indentation |
| **Filename extensions** | Lowercase: `.css`, `.js`, `.html`, `.json` |
| **File types** | ALL CAPS: `JPEG`, `PNG`, `SVG`, `MP4` |

### **International / Localization Parameters**

| Parameter | Rule |
|-----------|------|
| **Dates** | `June 9, 2025` (comma between day/year); `June 2025` (no comma) |
| **Times** | `10:45 a.m.`, `2:00 p.m.` (lowercase, periods, space before) |
| **Telephone** | `800-282-2732` (hyphens, no parentheses, no leading 1) |
| **Currency** | Consult international style guide |
| **Units** | Metric preferred; spell out in text, abbreviate in tables/specs |

### **CSS Class Naming Convention Derived from Guide**

```css
/* Based on Apple's hyphenation and capitalization rules */

/* Adjective compounds before noun */
.user-friendly-interface { }
.third-party-integration { }
.full-screen-modal { }
.drag-and-drop-zone { }

/* Predicate adjective (no hyphen) */
.is-user-friendly { }
.is-built-in { }

/* Product names: exact capitalization */
.apple-intelligence-badge { }
.m-series-chip-indicator { }
.vision-os-compatible { }  /* Note: visionOS in text, but CSS often lowercases */

/* Avoid blacklist/whitelist */
.deny-list { }
.allow-list { }

/* Accessibility */
.high-contrast-mode { }
.reduce-motion { }
.voiceover-compatible { }  /* Note: VoiceOver in text */

/* States using Apple terminology */
.is-turned-on { }      /* not .is-enabled */
.is-unavailable { }     /* not .is-disabled (for features) */
.is-selected { }       /* not .is-checked for generic */
```

### **JS Variable/Constant Naming**

```javascript
// Acronyms: all caps, no periods
const API_URL = '...';        // not ApiUrl
const HTML_CONTENT = '...';   // not HtmlContent

// Product names: match official style
const iCloudSync = '...';     // not IcloudSync
const macOSVersion = '...';   // not MacOSVersion or MacOsVersion
const airPodsModel = '...';   // not AirpodsModel

// Hyphenated compounds in camelCase
const userFriendly = true;    // from user-friendly
const thirdParty = true;      // from third-party
const builtIn = true;         // from built-in

// Avoid problematic terms
const denyList = [];          // not blacklist
const primaryBranch = 'main'; // not masterBranch
const placeholderData = {};   // not dummyData
const consistencyCheck = () => {}; // not sanityCheck
```

metadata:

Full rules live in `d:\IceBerg\DESIGN.MD`. This is a quick-reference summary of the additions extracted from the full Apple Style Guide (June 2025, 243 pages).

## Font terminology
- Always `font`, never `typeface`
- Always `font size` or `size`, never `type size`
- Always `font style` or `style`, never `type style` or `typestyle`

## Italic usage
- `italic` = adjective ("italic text"); `italics` = noun ("use italics")
- Use italics for: document titles, letters/words as themselves, emphasis (sparingly), placeholder names, variables, terms being defined
- Do NOT use italics for: text the user types (use quotes/code font), onscreen title-style element names

## Capitalization
- **UI labels, eyebrows, tags, footers** → sentence-style (first word + proper nouns only)
- **Button labels, section headings** → title-style (capitalize nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, conjunctions except coordinating, prepositions ≥5 letters)
- Title-style don't capitalize: `a`, `an`, `the`, `and`, `but`, `or`, `nor`, `for`, `yet`, `so`, `to` (infinitive), `as`, prepositions ≤4 letters
- Exception: always capitalize prepositions in phrasal verbs (`Turn On`, `Log In`, `Start Up`)

## Dashes
- Em dash (—): no spaces, close up to words — for interruption/aside
- En dash (–): no spaces, for number ranges and two-word compound adjectives
- Never use spaced em dashes ( — )

## Quotation marks
- Always curly/smart quotes in UI text (`"` `"`)
- Periods and commas inside closing quote
- Semicolons, colons, `?`, `!` outside unless part of quoted content
- Use italics (not quotes) for terms being defined

## Ellipsis
- Use single `…` character, not three dots `...`
- Omit trailing `…` from menu/button names when writing about them in prose

## Buttons & interactions
- Button labels: title-style caps always
- "Click a link" not "follow a link"
- "Click" (mouse), "press" (physical keys/buttons), "tap" (touchscreen)
- Never: "hit", "push", "type" for keys
- Never: "click on" — just "click"
- Never: "click and drag" — you click OR drag

## Web terminology
- `homepage` = entry point page only, not whole site; never `landing page` or `portal`
- `webpage` = one word
- `website` = whole collection
- `web` = lowercase
- `web app`, `web browser`, `web server` = two words
- `webcam`, `webcast`, `webmail`, `webpage`, `website` = one word

## Lists
- Always precede with a colon
- All items start with capital letter
- Complete-sentence items end with period; fragment items: consistent punctuation throughout

# Uriel — Auriel Solaris

Character portfolio site for **Uriel**, a Throne-class angel and the central figure of Auriel Solaris's two-timeline book series. Built as a single-page application with full client-side routing.

---

## Tech stack

| Tool | Version | Role |
|------|---------|------|
| [SolidJS](https://solidjs.com) | ^1.9.5 | UI framework |
| [@solidjs/router](https://github.com/solidjs/solid-router) | ^0.16.1 | Client-side routing |
| [Vite](https://vitejs.dev) | ^6.3.5 | Build tool & dev server |
| [vite-plugin-solid](https://github.com/solidjs/vite-plugin-solid) | ^2.11.6 | SolidJS Vite integration |
| TypeScript | via Vite | Type checking |

**Fonts** (Google Fonts): Playfair Display · Cormorant Garamond · Inter

---

## Project structure

```
IceBerg/
├── index.html              # Entry point — loads Google Fonts, mounts root
├── vite.config.ts          # Vite + SolidJS plugin config
├── tsconfig.json
├── package.json
│
├── src/
│   ├── index.tsx           # Router setup — all 6 routes defined here
│   ├── index.css           # Shared design tokens + page-header/footer classes
│   ├── vite-env.d.ts       # Vite client type reference (allows CSS imports)
│   │
│   ├── App.tsx             # Home page — three-column locked viewport layout
│   ├── home.css
│   │
│   └── pages/
│       ├── Timelines.tsx   # Two-timeline beat-by-beat comparison
│       ├── timelines.css
│       ├── Connections.tsx # Character web with filter + detail panel
│       ├── connections.css
│       ├── Books.tsx       # Published and forthcoming works
│       ├── books.css
│       ├── Worldbuilding.tsx  # Lore encyclopedia with sidebar nav
│       ├── worldbuilding.css
│       ├── Audience.tsx    # Contact / reach the author
│       └── audience.css
│
├── DESIGN.MD               # Full design guide — typography, CSS conventions, Apple style rules
├── CLAUDE.MD               # Claude Code project instructions
└── apple-style-guide.pdf   # Source reference — Apple Style Guide June 2025
```

---

## Pages

| Route | Page | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `/` | Home | Hero layout — Uriel's name, epithet, attributes, nav |
| `/timelines` | Timelines | Timeline A vs B beat cards with expandable detail |
| `/connections` | Connections | Filterable character cards with relationship panel |
| `/books` | Books | Four volumes across two timelines |
| `/worldbuilding` | Worldbuilding | Lore entries — dimensions, angels, hell, wings |
| `/audience` | Audience | Contact links for Auriel Solaris |

---

## Getting started

```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

Then open `http://localhost:5173`.

```bash
npm run build    # Output to dist/
npm run preview  # Preview the production build locally
```

---

## Design

The site follows a warm amber/gold palette (`#fffbf0` → `#78350f`) with a three-font system:

- **Playfair Display** — hero name only (weight 600 italic)
- **Cormorant Garamond** — all headings, titles, quotes, descriptions (weight 300–400)
- **Inter** — body text, labels, nav, UI elements (weight 400–600)

All CSS is split per page to prevent bloat. Shared tokens and layout classes live in `src/index.css`. Full conventions are documented in `DESIGN.MD`.

---

## Author

**Auriel Solaris** · [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/auriel.solaris) · [REDACTED_EMAIL]
